theme: The law’s true demand, heart-level obedience
readingInstruction: Read Matthew 5:21-48. Jesus takes six commands from the law and goes beneath the surface of each one. Notice the repeated phrase “You have heard that it was said… But I say to you.”
settingTheScene: Having said he came to fulfill the law, Jesus now shows what that means. The religious teachers of the day had narrowed the law to outward behavior, often with loopholes. Jesus takes six examples, murder, adultery, divorce, oaths, retaliation, and love for enemies, and shows that God’s law was always aimed at the heart. He does not set aside Moses. He reveals what Moses meant.
observation: “You have heard that it was said to those of old, You shall not murder… But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment” (5:21-22).

“So if you are offering your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar and go. First be reconciled to your brother” (5:23-24).
“Everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (5:28).
“If your right eye causes you to sin, tear it out and throw it away” (5:29).
“Let what you say be simply Yes or No” (5:37).
“But I say to you, Do not resist the one who is evil” (5:39).
“Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you” (5:44).
“You therefore must be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect” (5:48).
interpretation:
Each of the six examples follows the same pattern. Jesus quotes the commandment, and then he goes to the root. Murder starts in anger and contempt. Adultery starts in lust. Faithfulness in speech should not need oaths. Love should not stop at those who love us back. He is not adding new rules but exposing what the old ones always demanded.

The effect is meant to be unsettling. A person who thinks he has kept the law by avoiding murder finds that he has been angry. A person who has avoided adultery finds that he has looked with desire. No one can say, “I have kept all these.” Jesus has made the standard so high that everyone has to see that righteousness cannot be earned. That is why the Beatitudes began with the poor in spirit.

His strong language about tearing out an eye is not a command to self-harm but a way of saying that sin must be dealt with seriously, whatever it costs. And his teaching on retaliation points to a different way of living. Instead of getting even, his people absorb insult and give generously, trusting the Father to be their defender.

The last command is the most demanding: “Be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect.” The context is love for enemies. God sends rain and sun on the just and unjust alike, and his children are meant to look like him. “Perfect” here means whole, complete, not partial. Only one person has ever lived this out. That is why the Sermon drives us to Christ, who lived it for us and then gives his Spirit to begin forming it in us.
connection: 1 John 3:15 says everyone who hates his brother is a murderer. James 1:14-15 traces sin from desire to death. Proverbs 4:23 says to guard your heart. Romans 12:17-21 echoes Jesus on overcoming evil with good. Luke 23:34 shows Jesus praying for his enemies on the cross. Romans 5:8 says that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. Galatians 3:10-14 says Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law.
application:
Think of someone you are angry with. Ask what first step toward reconciliation God might want from you today.

Be honest about one area where outward obedience hides an inward struggle. Confess it to God, who already knows.

Pray for an enemy or a difficult person by name this week.
prayerPrompts: Confess the anger, desire, or love that stops short in you.
Thank Jesus for fulfilling the law you cannot.
Ask him to change your heart from the inside.
